clue.text: Container on vehicle not coming back

parts.note: a car is a common road vehicle

indicators.note: something coming back travels the opposite way, so the word is read from its end to its start

parts.note: taken as written, then turned around

explanation.surface: A shipping box sits on a lorry that has failed to return.
explanation.definitionFit: A carton is a cardboard box or packet used for holding goods, a kind of receptacle.

clue.text: The very last word in prayer!

definitions.text: The very last word in prayer!

parts.note: surface reading: the ultimate or most fashionable thing, the final say
setter's reading: literally the closing word spoken at the end of a prayer

explanation.walkthrough: 'The very last word' is an idiom for the latest fashion, but here it is meant literally: the word that ends a prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: Christians and Jews close prayers with this Hebrew affirmation meaning 'so be it', making it literally the final utterance.

clue.text: Try each sovereign brought in for treason

indicators.note: things brought in are placed inside something else, so these letters go within the outer word

parts.note: taken as written; it is split to hold the other pieces
taken as written
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword abbreviation for a queen or sovereign

explanation.surface: Putting each monarch on trial might be thought treasonous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' reads as a verb in the surface, but it is just the outer letters, split open to take the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Treachery is betrayal of trust, and treason is betrayal of one's country, so the two are close synonyms.

clue.text: Man's hat Ann repaired

indicators.note: a repaired item has been taken apart and put back together, so the letters are reassembled in a fresh order

parts.note: the six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man's hat has been mended by a woman called Ann.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is short for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay rather than showing possession.
explanation.definitionFit: Nathan is a male given name, so it is an example of a man, the usual crossword use of 'man'.

clue.text: Orders are: try US government department

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them, so the following letters are set out in a new sequence

parts.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A bossy instruction tells someone to attempt the United States government.
explanation.definitionFit: The Treasury is the ministry managing public finances in Britain and elsewhere, a branch of the state.

clue.text: Wanted to give someone a ring?

definitions.text: Wanted to give someone a ring?

parts.words: Wanted to give someone a ring
parts.note: surface reading: hoping to present a ring, as in a marriage proposal
setter's reading: 'give a ring' is British for making a call, and you need someone's digits for that

explanation.walkthrough: The engagement picture is the misdirection; 'give someone a ring' is everyday British for phoning them, and 'wanted' means needed.
explanation.definitionFit: To call someone you first require the string of digits assigned to their line, which is what is needed.

clue.text: Nearly, in goal, is surrounded

indicators.note: one word sits in the other, so the first set of letters goes inside the second

parts.note: an end is an aim or objective
close means almost or nearly there

explanation.surface: A footballer's shot nearly goes in but is crowded out by defenders.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a football goal, but goal here means an end or purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: Something enclosed is fenced or shut in on every side, which is what being surrounded means.

clue.text: Stops Scottish river vessel coming round

indicators.note: one thing coming round another encircles it, so the outer letters wrap the inner ones

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, the usual crossword vessel
the Tay is the longest river in Scotland

explanation.surface: A boat blocks a river in Scotland as it rounds a bend.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay is to halt or remain, and in law a stay of execution suspends proceedings, so stays matches stops as a verb.

clue.text: Exploding primers and rockets

indicators.note: an explosion scatters material everywhere, so the letters are blown apart and land in a new order

parts.note: the ten letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Detonating charges and fireworks go off together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rockets' looks like more fireworks alongside the primers, but in British slang a rocket is a severe telling-off.
explanation.definitionFit: In British informal speech a rocket is a sharp scolding, so rockets are stern rebukes from someone in authority.

clue.text: Stand beneath a statue

parts.note: surface reading: an instruction to go and wait under a monument
setter's reading: stand is a noun, a base on which a statue is mounted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' reads as a verb telling you where to wait, but it is a noun for a supporting base.
explanation.definitionFit: A plinth or base that raises a sculpture or column above the ground is exactly this kind of support.

clue.text: They stop motorists leaving car's front lights on

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening, so only its initial character is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word car's
lamps are lights

explanation.surface: A driver has left the headlights burning and something prevents them leaving.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain wheel clamps are fitted to illegally parked cars so the driver cannot drive away until a fine is paid.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheel clamps lock a parked car's wheel, so motorists cannot drive off until released by the authorities.

clue.text: Title of excellent vessel

parts.note: champion is informal for excellent, as in 'a champion idea'
a ship is a seagoing vessel

explanation.surface: A fine boat bears an impressive name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Title' suggests a name, but here it means a sporting crown.
explanation.definitionFit: In sport a title is the status of winner of a competition, so holding the title means winning the contest.

clue.text: Pens will be black at first, all with sharp ends

indicators.note: at first points to the very start of a word, so only its initial character is used

parts.note: the opening letter of the word black
taken as written
points are the sharp tips of things

explanation.surface: Pens will write in black to begin with, each with a fine nib.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballpoints are writing instruments using a tiny rolling ball to deliver ink, the commonest kind of pen today.

clue.text: Street map taking me round the labyrinth

indicators.note: to take something along is to hold it, so one set of letters holds the other
going round something encircles it, confirming which letters form the outside

parts.note: taken as written; it goes around the outside
the A-Z is a well-known British street atlas, originally of London

explanation.surface: Someone uses a street atlas to find their way through a confusing maze of streets.
explanation.walkthrough: The A-Z is a well-known British street atlas; 'me' goes round it rather than the map holding 'me'.
explanation.definitionFit: A labyrinth is an intricate network of paths designed to confuse, which is a synonym for this puzzle.

clue.text: It's worn out, having to cover a new building

definitions.note: a cryptic description: a garment worn outdoors, over other clothes

indicators.note: a new building is constructed afresh, so the letters are put together in a different structure

parts.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Something is exhausted after having to cover a newly built structure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worn out' looks like 'exhausted' but means worn outside, as a garment is worn outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy coat put on over other clothing when going outdoors is literally a garment for wearing outside.

clue.text: Angry with news feature in most newspapers

parts.note: cross means annoyed or angry
word means news or information, as in 'any word?'

explanation.surface: Readers are furious about a news story that appears across the press.
explanation.definitionFit: Almost every daily paper carries a grid puzzle of clues and answers, a regular section like this very one.

clue.text: Rearranged side beat health problem

indicators.note: rearranging means putting into a different order, so these letters are sorted afresh

parts.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A team reshuffled its line-up and beat a medical setback.
explanation.definitionFit: Diabetes is a chronic medical condition affecting blood sugar regulation, a common illness.

clue.text: Most popular school period?

parts.note: surface reading: the favourite lesson in the timetable
setter's reading: the break when pupils go outdoors to run around, which children love best

explanation.walkthrough: 'Period' suggests a lesson, but the favourite part of the school day is the break between lessons.
explanation.definitionFit: Children's recess, the break when pupils go out to the playground, is reliably the best-loved part of the day.

clue.text: Scraps rum on 1st September

parts.note: rum is old British slang for strange or odd

indicators.note: 1st points to the opening position of the word, so only that character is used

parts.note: the opening letter of the word September

explanation.surface: Leftover rum is drunk on the first day of September.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink, but in British usage it also means peculiar.
explanation.definitionFit: In 'odds and ends' the word means bits and pieces, small leftover items like scraps.

clue.text: A second drink for a horse?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a drink taken straight after another, such as beer after a spirit
second meaning: a steeplechaser, a horse that races over fences

explanation.surface: Someone orders another round to toast a racehorse.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a follow-up drink taken after a shot and a jumping racehorse in steeplechases.

clue.text: Bathroom cleaners?

parts.note: surface reading: products or people that scrub a bathroom
setter's reading: the things kept in the bathroom for cleaning teeth

explanation.walkthrough: The bathroom is where the cleaning happens, not what gets cleaned.
explanation.definitionFit: These bristled implements are kept by the basin and used to clean teeth, so they are cleaners in the bathroom.

clue.text: Subject: "The Crossword Compiler"

parts.note: taken as written
the setter refers to themself, so the compiler is me

explanation.surface: A title-like heading announcing a talk about the puzzle setter.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the topic or main idea of a piece of writing or discussion.

clue.text: Girl once bought things in India

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a female given name
second meaning: a former Indian coin worth a sixteenth of a rupee

explanation.surface: A young woman used to go shopping in India.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna is a girl's name and also an old copper coin of British India, money that once paid for goods there.

clue.text: Possibly fly in with a religious group

parts.note: taken as written
a sect is a religious group

explanation.surface: Perhaps someone flies in alongside members of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' marks fly as an example: a fly is one kind of the creature wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A housefly is one example of a small six-legged invertebrate, hence 'possibly' in the definition.

clue.text: Singer soon gets into these instruments

indicators.note: what gets into something ends up inside it, so these letters are placed within the other word

parts.note: a bass is a singer with the lowest male voice
taken as written; it goes inside

explanation.surface: A vocalist will shortly take up woodwind instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: Bassoons are large double-reed woodwind instruments with a deep tone, members of the orchestra.

clue.text: Fool tossed roses to valuer

parts.note: an ass is a fool

indicators.note: things tossed are thrown about and land jumbled, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A silly person throws flowers to an appraiser.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessor estimates the worth of property, for taxation or insurance, so is a professional appraiser.

clue.text: Air lad put into one sort of tyre

indicators.note: the letters are put into a new form, recast into a different shape

parts.note: the six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A boy pumps air into a tyre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put into' looks like inserting one thing in another, but nothing goes inside; the letters are reshaped.
explanation.definitionFit: A radial is a tyre whose internal cords run at right angles to the tread, a standard construction for car tyres.
